extracted.intended_audience: readers of Cory Doctorow's Little Brother; young adults and activists interested in digital activism and media-engagement tactics
extracted.subtask_description: Organizing and running a press conference inside a multiplayer online game to engage journalists, protect participants, and publicize activist content. Includes site/time selection, messaging, privacy considerations, delegation, and use of in-game mechanics to manage reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose neutral/no-combat location
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick a trading post where there's no PvP allowed (neutral ground) so reporters aren't at risk of being killed in-game.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator picks Patcheye Pete's Market because it's nearest the spawn area and is a no-PvP zone; neutral ground lets reporters attend without being attacked and makes crowd control easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pick an accessible time
rubrics_metrics.description: Schedule the event at a time when people can attend (e.g., 8PM after dinner).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator chose 8PM after dinner to maximize attendance and to coordinate with others' schedules; factor in audience timezones and family/real-life obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicize and invite press clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Email the press with invitations and instructions on how to join; expect varied responses and some requests for technical support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator emails multiple outlets, notes that responses range from puzzled to enthusiastic, and that many reporters want tech support for signing onto the game. Provide clear joining instructions and offer setup help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare a concise opening statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft a clear opening message that states who you are and why you're there; paste it into chat for quick dissemination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marcus wrote and pasted a prepared statement explaining his position and beliefs; drafting with collaborators (Ange) and testing wording beforehand helps ensure clarity under fast chat conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use text/chat to avoid misquotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer written chat for replies because text is easier to follow and can't be misquoted as easily as voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator chooses text over voice because many people talking at once would be confusing and text reduces the risk of being misquoted by journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowd-source answers and delegate
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow community members to answer questions; if overwhelmed or tired, hand the keyboard to others to continue the engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marcus lets Xnetters respond to questions and later hands the keyboard to Ange when tired; plan for multiple spokespeople and distributed answering to handle volume and varied questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignore hostile or unwanted questions
rubrics_metrics.description: If you don't like a question, ignore it — others can answer instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ange advises Marcus to ignore questions he doesn't like; establishing this rule ahead of time prevents derailing the event and keeps messaging on-topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use community helpers to locate/reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask experienced players to identify newcomers (reporters) and guide them to the meeting spot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Xnetters were told to hang out on the route and direct disoriented reporters to Patcheye Pete's; leverage community familiarity with the game to shepherd attendees and provide on-the-ground (in-game) assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate mixed press attitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect journalists to be sympathetic, hostile, or puzzled; prepare for a range of questions and tones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marcus encounters sympathetic and hostile reporters; train spokespeople to respond calmly, be honest, and know when to de-escalate or defer to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect identity and privacy where necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider declining on-the-record interviews or insisting on masking/anonymity if participation carries risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marcus receives offers from news organizations and decides to decline interviews for privacy reasons; a reporter offers to mask identity, but participants should evaluate risk (e.g., potential adversarial actors posing as reporters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer technical support for press participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared to help reporters sign into the game and navigate the environment; many will need assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists asked for tech support to join Clockwork Plunder; assign community tech helpers and prepare step-by-step joining instructions or remote setup assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use aggregated online content to drive media interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect, categorize, and publish evidence (videos, photos) about abuses to create a narrative and make the story easy for media to follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marcus creates an AbusesOfAuthority category, posts the General Geist video, updates entries with IDs and context, and aggregates submissions; maintain organized archives and provide source links to reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic objective: embarrass rather than physically oppose
rubrics_metrics.description: When lacking superior force, use public exposure and ridicule to make opponents look incompetent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ange advises that the goal is to embarrass the DHS because you can't out-shoot them; craft messaging and evidence that highlights incompetence or abuse to win public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft honest, reflective answers
rubrics_metrics.description: Answer questions honestly, admit uncertainty, and explain reasoning rather than making unfounded claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marcus answers honestly when asked about DHS efficacy ('I don't know...'), explaining his reasoning about freedom and safety; honest, thoughtful responses can resonate more than bluster.
